nameStory: Desert goosefoot gets its common name from two sources: 'desert' reflects its natural home in the dry western regions of North America, while 'goosefoot' comes from the distinctive shape of many plants in this family - their leaves often resemble the webbed foot of a goose. The scientific name Chenopodium literally means 'goose foot' in Greek, cementing this whimsical connection between plant and waterfowl.
description: Desert goosefoot is a small annual herb that typically grows 2-3 feet tall, sometimes developing branches as it matures. This western native has somehow found its way to New England, though it's extremely rare here with only one recorded sighting. The plant has an unusual powdery or dusty texture that makes it feel almost chalky to the touch, especially on the leaves and flower clusters. Its oval to lance-shaped leaves give it away as a member of the goosefoot family, and tiny flowers cluster together in dense, inconspicuous groups.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive powdery, chalky texture that feels dusty when you rub them between your fingers. Some leaves may have small lobes along their edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, greenish flowers packed into small, dense clusters that appear both where leaves meet the stem and at the tips of branches. No showy petals - just minute, inconspicuous blooms.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Annual herb reaching 2-3 feet tall, sometimes branching. The entire plant has an overall dusty, grayish-green appearance that sets it apart from most other weedy plants.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Distinctly powdery or mealy texture throughout, especially noticeable on leaves and flower clusters. This chalky coating can often be rubbed off with your fingers.

habitat: In its native range, desert goosefoot thrives in open, dry habitats with alkaline soils, often growing alongside sagebrush in western landscapes. Since it's been spotted only once in New England, it likely appeared in disturbed, open ground - perhaps along roadsides, in vacant lots, or other areas with poor, compacted soil. Look for it in sunny spots where few other plants can establish, particularly areas that might have alkaline conditions.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants begin growing as temperatures warm, developing their characteristic powdery leaves early in the season.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their tiny flower clusters throughout the warm months. The dusty texture becomes most pronounced during hot, dry weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowers develop into small seeds before the plant dies back with the first hard frost, completing its annual cycle.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain - this annual plant survives only as seeds in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: Desert goosefoot is so adapted to alkaline soils that it can actually help indicate where the ground has high salt content - Native American peoples traditionally used the presence of goosefoot plants to locate areas where they could harvest natural salt deposits for food preservation and trading.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with common lambsquarters, its much more common relative in New England. The key difference is the pronounced powdery coating on desert goosefoot - lambsquarters may have some dustiness, but nothing like the chalky, mealy texture of desert goosefoot. Remember: if it feels like you dipped it in flour, you might have found the rare desert species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting an arid plant, desert goosefoot isn't actually restricted to true deserts - it just prefers the dry, open conditions common in western North America. Its appearance in New England is so unusual that any sighting would be botanically significant and worth reporting to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Desert goosefoot stands out from other New England goosefoots primarily by its exceptionally powdery texture - much more pronounced than the light dustiness of common lambsquarters or other relatives. While lambsquarters leaves often have whitish undersides, desert goosefoot's entire plant appears grayish and chalky. The leaf shapes are similar across the genus, but desert goosefoot's adaptation to alkaline soils gives it that distinctive mealy coating that's hard to miss once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common lambsquarters is much more widespread than its relatives like pitseed goosefoot or fig-leaved goosefoot in New England.
Among New England goosefoots, pitseed goosefoot stands out for its strongly toothed lower leaves and honeycomb-pitted seeds.
Fogg's goosefoot is distinguished from Common Lambsquarters by having more triangular, less elongated leaves and typically being smaller overall.
Unlike common lambsquarters which has simple diamond or triangular leaves, fig-leaved goosefoot has deeply divided, lobed leaves that are unmistakable.
Tree spinach dwarfs its goosefoot relatives like common lambsquarters, which rarely exceed 3-4 feet tall and have much thinner stems.
Unlike the common lambsquarters with its plain green leaves dusted with white powder, striped goosefoot has those unmistakable light stripes running through each leaf.
